web_evidence.title: The Young Lions — University of Chicago Press authorized excerpt
web_evidence.note: The sustained, permission-reprinted Chapter One excerpt narrates Margaret Freemantle externally as 'she' while entering her perceptions and thoughts, establishing third-person narration for the opening.

web_evidence.title: Exploring Satire in the Early Postmodern American War Novel
web_evidence.note: Kolby Elizabeth Brown's Montana State University MA thesis explicitly identifies The Young Lions as using an omniscient narrator and analyzes that narrator across interior passages.

web_evidence.title: The Young Lions — Google Books / University of Chicago Press edition
web_evidence.note: Publisher metadata describes Shaw as telling the story through the viewpoints of three named characters—Christian, Michael, and Noah—corroborating a multi-focal rather than participating narrator structure.

web_evidence.title: A Few More Reflections on Irwin Shaw's The Young Lions
web_evidence.note: Novelist Helen Lowe's structural discussion reports that Chapter One follows Margaret and the remainder is told through Christian, Noah, and Michael, with character thoughts presented from their respective viewpoints.

person_note: The book uses third-person narration with shifting focalization among Margaret in the opening and principally Christian, Noah, and Michael thereafter. The authorized opening, a scholarly whole-book analysis explicitly naming an omniscient narrator, publisher structural metadata, and interior Goodreads passages such as q00389 and q00394 agree. First-person material in q00379 and q00381 is therefore local character discourse, while the 'I' in q00389 is explicitly Michael's direct thought; none establishes a sustained first-person section. The remaining uncertainty is only the missing immediate attribution around those two clipped monologues, not the book-level person.
